content:
I was looking into trying to prove some facts about well quasi ordering (namely that if a relation is Well Quasi Ordered then a set based version of the relation is Well quasi ordered) and I noticed I had to assume that my relation was a preorder even though I believe this is not necessary for the proof.

I wanted to use the fact that every sequence within a WQO (well quasi order) has a monotone subsequence, which I also think does not need a preorder property, 

theorem WellQuasiOrdered.exists_monotone_subseq [IsPreorder α r] (h : WellQuasiOrdered r)
    (f : ℕ → α) : ∃ g : ℕ ↪o ℕ, ∀ m n, m ≤ n → r (f (g m)) (f (g n))

if I remove the assumption then theorem ends up breaking because it relies on 

/-- This is the infinitary Erdős–Szekeres theorem, and an important lemma in the usual proof of
Bolzano-Weierstrass for `ℝ`. -/
theorem exists_increasing_or_nonincreasing_subseq (r : α → α → Prop) [IsTrans α r] (f : ℕ → α) :
    ∃ g : ℕ ↪o ℕ,
      (∀ m n : ℕ, m < n → r (f (g m)) (f (g n))) ∨ ∀ m n : ℕ, m < n → ¬r (f (g m)) (f (g n)) := by

Which directly uses IsTrans α r in the proof.

This shouldn't be necessary as you should be able to colour the edges between each pair of Numbers based on whether the relation is true for them, and then use the Infinite Ramsey theorem to get an infinite clique of increasing or non-increasing numbers.

Now it looks like someone has used Lean (possibly not lean 4) to prove a version of this here https://github.com/b-mehta/combinatorics/blob/extras/src/inf_ramsey.lean , so I'm wondering if there's a reason this has been left out of MathLib itself?\

Now it looks like there was a discussion of this earlier this year here #new members > Is the infinitary Ramsey theorem in mathlib? but it doesn't look like any of the referenced PRs have been merged

For uses in my automata theory project, I proved Ramsey's theorem for infinite graphs in Lean4:
https://github.com/ctchou/AutomataTheory/blob/main/AutomataTheory/Mathlib/InfGraphRamsey.lean
which should suffice for your purpose.

I have an updated version of that code for Lean 4, which I can post later in the week, which gives a short proof of the infinite Ramsey theorem for hypergraphs. But I agree that the theorem you quote should be true without transitivity. The linked Lean 3 code wasn't ported or updated because it uses a weird recursion principle which mathlib at the time didn't want, and with the benefit of (several) years of hindsight, is not the right way of proving it.
Ive been working on incorporating ramsey theory in my own transform theory work - ill keep an eye on this. Thanks for the heads up
@Bhavik Mehta Just wondering if your code will be available soon. Thanks in advance!

Reviving this — it's exactly what I need downstream, and I'd like to help get it in mathlib4.

I'm formalizing my own work on well-quasi-order / BQO
(https://github.com/yannpequignot/lean-wqo-continuous-functions)
whose proof relies on infinite Ramsey for arity 2 and 3 (so far, but the BQO version of the result requires Nash-Williams' transfinite generalization to fronts or barriers), so I have strong motivation for it landing.

I also have ready downstream uses
(https://github.com/yannpequignot/TwoBQO)
including the transitivity-free WellQuasiOrdered.exists_monotone_subseq that @Leo Shine raised.

theorem WellQuasiOrdered.exists_monotone_subseq_lt (h : WellQuasiOrdered r) (f : ℕ → α) :
    ∃ e : ℕ → ℕ, StrictMono e ∧ ∀ m n : ℕ, m < n → r (f (e m)) (f (e n)) := by

I was surprised that WellQuasiOrdered is defined in mathlib for an arbitrary relation (contrarily to what the name suggests). As @Bhavik Mehta noted it should be, this holds without transitivity — in fact exists_monotone_subseq_lt assumes no order axioms whatsoever. The only price is weakening the conclusion from m ≤ n to m < n: the ≤ form needs reflexivity just for the diagonal m = n, nothing more.

I had a look at PRs related to this statement which keep stalling.
• #12773 (@Peter Nelson) : merge conflicts, then inactive;
Fin k ↪o encoding, adds to Order.Extension.Linear.
• #27217 (@Ching-Tsun Chou) , large-import, merge conflicts . Closed.
• @Bhavik Mehta mentioned a short Lean 4 hypergraph proof that's "the right way" —
did that get posted anywhere? I couldn't find it.

I am happy to help moving this. Whatever the group prefers, I can help with either:

  1. Adopt #12773, do the mechanical finishing, and stay on it through review.
  2. A self-contained general-arity proof I already have (induction on arity via the
    fan argument), here:
    (https://github.com/yannpequignot/lean-infinite-ramsey)
    It's deliberately minimal — only Fintype.Pigeonhole, Nat.Lattice, Nat.Nth,
    no dependency PRs, no edits to other files — precisely to sidestep the
    large-import / blocked-by-other-PR issues that stalled the earlier attempts.

I currently use a Finset ℕ (card = r) colouring interface, following Mehta's Lean 3
inf_ramsey.lean; I see the prior PRs went with Fin k ↪o.

"@Bhavik Mehta  — if your hypergraph proof is close, I'm glad to just help land it; otherwise, adopt #12773 or a fresh minimal PR?"

Full disclosure: this development is AI-assisted. I understand and stand behind every statement, I'm really eager to learn more about Mathlib LEAN standards and I'm offering to do the human review and maintenance work — not to drop generated code on anyone.

I should point out that #27217 is not really my own work, but my attempt at reviving earlier works by @Peter Nelson:
#new members > Is the infinitary Ramsey theorem in mathlib?
Please take a look at the last comment I left in #27217.

@Ching-Tsun Chou thanks for the clarification, I fixed the mention to credit @Peter Nelson's work . The new members thread is relevant too, thank you. Given your last comment in #27217, it would appear that most of all we are really waiting to settle for the right proof strategy.

On that: @Bhavik Mehta, in #27217 you noted it's cleaner to do this "in terms of
finsets directly, and then a version for order-embeddings if needed". My
self-contained proof (linked above) is exactly that — a Finset ℕ (card = r)
colouring interface, minimal imports, no dependency PRs. Happy to shape it into a
PR along those lines if that's the direction you'd prefer and work on the version for order-embeddings if needed.

@Bhavik Mehta — out of curiosity, does the approach you have in mind extend to
the transfinite case (Nash-Williams for fronts/barriers)? That's ultimately what my
BQO work needs downstream, so I'm interested whether the "right way" generalizes
there — though landing the finite-arity version first is clearly the priority.
